title: New Fabric "Plant Armor" Helps Strawberries Grow More Fruit
summary:
Strawberry plants are often attacked by insects, and farmers may use pesticides, which are chemicals that kill pests, to protect them. Researchers at North Carolina State University have developed a new fabric called Plant Armor that may help.

The fabric is placed directly over strawberry plants. Its three-dimensional structure forms a barrier that keeps insects from reaching the plants. The layered material still lets sunlight, rain and air pass through.

In tunnel field tests, strawberries covered by Plant Armor produced yields as much as 3.56 times higher than plants with no cover. The researchers say the fabric did not reduce light or harm the plants' health. Gabriel Olawuyi, a graduate research assistant and the lead author of the study, had expected a problem. He said, "To produce fruit, plants need sunlight," so the team thought a darker cover might make plants grow more stems and leaves instead of fruit. But the fabric did not block the light, and fruit production went up a lot.

The fabric also kept the plants a little warmer during all three growing seasons of the study. That extra warmth helped covered plants reach the fruiting stage earlier. Because the fabric stops insects from feeding on the plants, Olawuyi said it could also reduce how much pesticide farmers need. The researchers say it may also help reduce water use.

The story behind the idea is surprising. Plant Armor grew out of research on making military uniforms more resistant to mosquito bites and making body armor more comfortable for soldiers. The study was published in the journal Agriculture.
why_it_matters: If farmers can protect fruit from insects with a cover instead of more chemicals, they may grow more food with fewer pesticides.
